description: We are Carlos and Ramon, the team behind Gaia Symphony. We combine an interest in technology, space and creative storytelling to explore how Earth data can become an accessible sound experience. Carlos focuses on the project concept and digital experience, while Ramon explores sound design and scientific communication. We welcome curious minds interested in sonification, Earth science and inclusive design.
summary:
Gaia Symphony is a concept for an accessible Earth Jukebox that pairs NASA Earth Information Center visualizations with sound generated in real time. Users would choose a topic, explore a timeline and hear how the underlying information changes.

Clearly explained mappings would translate values into pitch and distinguish data layers through different tones, while keeping audio synchronized with the visuals. Keyboard navigation, spoken explanations and text alternatives would support different access needs.

We developed a project concept and a seven-slide presentation describing the user experience, proposed sonification rules and a temperature-anomaly use case based on NASA resources. No working application or audio engine has been implemented, and no datasets have been processed.

The intended impact is to help more people explore Earth science through complementary visual, auditory and textual experiences.
details:
PROJECT CONCEPT

Gaia Symphony proposes an accessible way to explore Earth science by listening to information alongside NASA visualizations. It responds to The Earth Information Jukebox challenge with a concept for synchronized, interactive sonification.

THE USER EXPERIENCE

Users would select an Earth Information Center visualization, learn what its sounds represent and explore its timeline. Playback controls would let them pause, revisit a date and compare different moments using the same sound scale. Each track would explain its source, units and time period.

HOW IT WOULD WORK

A future implementation would associate visualization frames with matching numerical values and timestamps. A browser audio engine would generate sound dynamically during playback.

Higher values could produce higher pitches. Different data layers could use distinct tones, while stereo position could indicate location. Missing values would trigger an explicit cue rather than being represented as zero. An audible reference and fixed mapping scales would help users interpret comparisons.

If only image frames were available, any sound derived from image properties would be identified as image sonification. It would not be presented as a direct measurement of physical conditions.

NASA EXAMPLE

The presentation uses NASA’s Global Temperature Anomalies from 1880 to 2024 visualization as a reference case. The proposed experience would connect temperature anomalies to pitch while preserving the visualization’s dates, units and baseline. Implementation would require matching the data’s spatial and temporal aggregation to the visual frames.

ACCESSIBILITY AND INTENDED IMPACT

The design proposes keyboard navigation, screen-reader labels, spoken explanations, readable text, adjustable sound and a mono option. Visual and textual alternatives would remain available for people who cannot or prefer not to use audio.

Potential settings include classrooms, museums and independent learning. These benefits remain hypotheses requiring evaluation with users.

PROPOSED TECHNOLOGY

A possible implementation would use HTML, CSS and JavaScript, browser audio synthesis and a preprocessing step to align data with visualization frames. These technologies describe a possible architecture, not software already developed.

CURRENT DELIVERABLE

The completed deliverable is a seven-slide concept presentation defining the experience, sound mappings and accessibility goals. No application, audio engine or data pipeline has been implemented. No datasets have been processed and no user testing has taken place.
